title: 01 — Training and Evaluation from Scratch
html:
01 — Training and Evaluation from Scratch

The one idea: training is just repeatedly nudging numbers to reduce an error measure on past data. The hard part is proving the model works on data it has never seen. Split first, scale with training statistics only, pick metrics that respect rare events, and distrust any result that looks too good.

1. What it is

Supervised learning: you have examples with inputs (features, X) and a known answer (label, y), and you fit a function that maps one to the other.

  • Classification predicts a category: will this issuer be downgraded, yes or no?
  • Regression predicts a number: next month's fund flow.

Logistic regression is the simplest serious classifier. It computes a weighted sum of the features and squashes it into a probability between 0 and 1 with the sigmoid function 1 / (1 + e^-z).

.NET comparison: a trained model is a pure function whose constants were found by an optimiser instead of written by hand.

2. Why it matters

  • In finance, the event you care about is rare: defaults and downgrades are a few percent of cases. Accuracy is then meaningless, because "never" is 97% accurate.
  • Decisions use the probability (for pricing, provisioning, review queues), so probabilities must be calibrated.
  • Leakage (using information not available at prediction time) is the most common reason a model that worked in development fails in production.

3. The main ideas, beginner to expert

3.1 Beginner: how training works

  1. Start with weights of zero.
  2. Forward pass: compute a predicted probability for every row.
  3. Loss: measure how wrong the predictions are. For classification, use log-loss (cross-entropy): confident wrong answers cost a lot.
  4. Gradient: compute, for each weight, which direction reduces the loss. For logistic regression it is Xᵀ(p − y) / n.
  5. Step: move each weight a little in that direction (the learning rate). Repeat.

Regularisation (L2) adds a small penalty on large weights, so the model prefers simpler explanations and overfits less.

3.2 Intermediate: splitting and scaling

---
title: Data splits and where each statistic may come from
---
flowchart LR
    D["All labelled data"] --> TR["Train (60%)<br/>fit weights, scaling stats"]
    D --> VA["Validation (20%)<br/>choose settings and threshold"]
    D --> TE["Test (20%)<br/>report once, at the end"]
    TR -. "mean and std for scaling" .-> VA
    TR -. "same mean and std" .-> TE
  • Train: fit the model, and compute any statistics (scaling means, category encodings) here only.
  • Validation: compare settings and choose the decision threshold.
  • Test: touch once, to report. Every extra look turns it into a second validation set.
  • Cross-validation: rotate the validation fold k times when data is scarce.
  • Time-ordered data: split by time, never randomly (see 04).
  • Groups: if one issuer has many rows, keep each issuer in one split only.

3.3 Intermediate: metrics for rare events

Metric Answers Use when
ROC AUC How well does the model rank positives above negatives? 0.5 = random, 1 = perfect Comparing models independent of threshold
Precision Of the cases flagged, how many were right? Review capacity is limited
Recall Of the true cases, how many were flagged? Missing a case is costly
PR AUC Precision-recall trade-off across thresholds Very rare positives
Brier score Mean squared error of probabilities Probability quality
Calibration table Predicted vs observed rate per bucket Probabilities drive money or capacity

The threshold is a business decision: set it from review capacity and the cost of a miss versus a false alarm, never by leaving it at 0.5.

3.4 Expert: calibration and leakage

  • Calibration: a model can rank well (high AUC) but be over-confident. Fix it with Platt scaling or isotonic regression, fitted on validation data, and check it per segment.

  • Leakage patterns:

    • features recorded after the label event (a "watch" flag set after the downgrade),
    • aggregates computed over the whole dataset,
    • duplicated entities across splits,
    • random splits on time series.

    The symptom is a score that is too good. The cure is point-in-time feature construction (02).

4. Working code

The script trains logistic regression by gradient descent on made-up issuer data (about 3% downgrades). It evaluates with AUC, precision and recall at several thresholds and a calibration table, then shows how a leaked feature inflates AUC. numpy only.

import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(7)
# Made-up data: will a bond issuer be downgraded within a year? Two features, about 3% positives.
n = 4000
leverage = rng.normal(3.0, 1.0, n)                 # debt / EBITDA
coverage = rng.normal(4.0, 1.5, n)                 # interest coverage
logit = -4.2 + 0.9 * (leverage - 3) - 0.7 * (coverage - 4)
y = (rng.random(n) < 1 / (1 + np.exp(-logit))).astype(float)
X = np.column_stack([leverage, coverage])

# 1. Split BEFORE looking at anything: train 60%, validation 20%, test 20%.
idx = rng.permutation(n)
tr, va, te = idx[:2400], idx[2400:3200], idx[3200:]
mu, sd = X[tr].mean(0), X[tr].std(0)               # scaling statistics from TRAIN only (no leakage)
Z = (X - mu) / sd

# 2. Logistic regression trained by gradient descent: the whole algorithm in a few lines.
def fit(Z, y, lr=0.1, epochs=2000, l2=0.01):
    w, b = np.zeros(Z.shape[1]), 0.0
    for _ in range(epochs):
        p = 1 / (1 + np.exp(-(Z @ w + b)))           # predicted probability
        grad_w = Z.T @ (p - y) / len(y) + l2 * w     # gradient of log-loss (+ L2 penalty)
        grad_b = (p - y).mean()
        w, b = w - lr * grad_w, b - lr * grad_b
    return w, b
predict = lambda Z, w, b: 1 / (1 + np.exp(-(Z @ w + b)))
w, b = fit(Z[tr], y[tr])
print("weights (scaled features):", np.round(w, 3), "bias:", round(b, 3))

# 3. Metrics that matter when positives are rare.
def auc(y, p):                                      # probability a random positive outranks a random negative
    order = np.argsort(p)
    ranks = np.empty(len(p)); ranks[order] = np.arange(1, len(p) + 1)
    pos = y == 1
    return (ranks[pos].sum() - pos.sum() * (pos.sum() + 1) / 2) / (pos.sum() * (~pos).sum())
def precision_recall(y, p, t):
    pred = p >= t
    tp = (pred & (y == 1)).sum()
    return tp / max(pred.sum(), 1), tp / (y == 1).sum()
p_va = predict(Z[va], w, b)
print(f"validation: positives {int(y[va].sum())}/{len(va)}, AUC {auc(y[va], p_va):.3f}, "
      f"accuracy if we always say 'no' {1 - y[va].mean():.3f}")
for t in (0.5, 0.2, 0.1):
    pr, rc = precision_recall(y[va], p_va, t)
    print(f"  threshold {t}: precision {pr:.2f}, recall {rc:.2f}")

# 4. Calibration: do predicted probabilities match observed rates? Brier score = mean squared error.
p_te = predict(Z[te], w, b)
bins = np.quantile(p_te, [0, .5, .8, .95, 1])
for lo, hi in zip(bins[:-1], bins[1:]):
    m = (p_te >= lo) & (p_te <= hi)
    print(f"  predicted {p_te[m].mean():.3f} vs observed {y[te][m].mean():.3f}  ({m.sum()} issuers)")
print(f"test AUC {auc(y[te], p_te):.3f}, Brier {np.mean((p_te - y[te]) ** 2):.4f}")

# 5. Leakage: a feature that secretly contains the answer looks brilliant and is worthless.
leak = y + rng.normal(0, 0.3, n)                    # e.g. "rating outlook revised" recorded AFTER the downgrade
ZL = np.column_stack([Z, (leak - leak[tr].mean()) / leak[tr].std()])
wl, bl = fit(ZL[tr], y[tr])
print(f"with a leaked feature: validation AUC {auc(y[va], predict(ZL[va], wl, bl)):.3f}  <- too good to be true")

Output:

weights (scaled features): [ 0.759 -0.788] bias: -3.853
validation: positives 24/800, AUC 0.813, accuracy if we always say 'no' 0.970
  threshold 0.5: precision 0.00, recall 0.00
  threshold 0.2: precision 0.44, recall 0.17
  threshold 0.1: precision 0.16, recall 0.38
  predicted 0.011 vs observed 0.005  (400 issuers)
  predicted 0.033 vs observed 0.021  (240 issuers)
  predicted 0.079 vs observed 0.042  (120 issuers)
  predicted 0.189 vs observed 0.175  (40 issuers)
test AUC 0.794, Brier 0.0215
with a leaked feature: validation AUC 0.998  <- too good to be true

What to notice:

  • Always saying "no" is 97% accurate, and catches nothing. AUC (0.813) is the honest ranking measure.
  • At the default 0.5 threshold the model flags nobody. Lowering it to 0.1 catches 38% of downgrades at 16% precision. Which threshold is right depends on how many cases analysts can review.
  • The calibration table shows mild over-prediction in the middle buckets (0.079 predicted vs 0.042 observed). If the probabilities drive provisioning, recalibrate.
  • The leaked feature pushes AUC to 0.998. Any result like this should trigger a search for leakage, not a celebration.

The same in scikit-learn (not run: scikit-learn wasn't installed in the build environment):

# Not run.
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.metrics import roc_auc_score, brier_score_loss
model = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), LogisticRegression(C=100.0, max_iter=1000))   # scaler fitted on train only
model.fit(X_train, y_train)
p = model.predict_proba(X_test)[:, 1]
print(roc_auc_score(y_test, p), brier_score_loss(y_test, p))

The pipeline guarantees the scaler is fitted only on the data passed to fit, which prevents a classic leak.

5. Common mistakes

  1. Scaling or encoding on all data before splitting. Test information leaks into training.
  2. Reporting accuracy on rare events. Use AUC, PR AUC, precision and recall at a chosen threshold.
  3. Tuning on the test set. It stops being a test.
  4. Leaving the threshold at 0.5. Choose it from costs and capacity.
  5. Random splits on time series or repeated entities. Split by time or by group.

6. Exercise (1.5 hours)

  1. Add 5-fold cross-validation to the script, and report the mean and spread of AUC.
  2. Implement Platt scaling: fit a one-feature logistic regression on validation predictions, and compare the calibration tables before and after.
  3. Choose a threshold that gives 50 flagged issuers per 800, and report its precision and recall.

7. Questions to test yourself

  1. What does the gradient tell the optimiser?
  2. Why must scaling statistics come from the training split only?
  3. Why is accuracy misleading at a 3% positive rate?
  4. What does AUC measure, in one sentence?
  5. Name three common sources of leakage.

Answers

  1. For each weight, the direction and size of change that reduces the loss fastest.
  2. Otherwise information from validation or test data shapes the model, and the evaluation becomes optimistic.
  3. Predicting "no" for everyone already scores 97% while catching nothing.
  4. The probability that a randomly chosen positive gets a higher score than a randomly chosen negative.
  5. Features recorded after the event, statistics computed on all data, and the same entity appearing in both train and test (random time splits are a fourth).

8. Sources
